title: Carl Jung: Analytical Psychology
overview: Carl Jung began as Freud's chosen successor but built his own theory, analytical psychology. He broadened libido into a general psychic energy governed by the principles of opposites, equivalence and entropy; argued that the future shapes personality as much as the past; and placed even more weight on the unconscious, adding a collective unconscious of inherited archetypes such as the persona, anima/animus, shadow and self. His typology of attitudes (introversion, extraversion) and functions (thinking, feeling, sensing, intuiting) produced eight psychological types and later the MBTI. Jung saw middle age as the crucial period of development, when energy turns inward toward individuation. The chapter covers his life, theory, assessment methods, research support and an evaluation of his contributions and criticisms.
objectives: Explain the three major points on which Jung's analytical psychology differed from Freud's psychoanalysis.
Describe how Jung's childhood and midlife crisis shaped his theory.
Explain Jung's concept of psychic energy and the principles of opposites, equivalence and entropy.
Describe the ego, the two attitudes, the four functions and the eight psychological types.
Distinguish the personal unconscious and complexes from the collective unconscious and archetypes.
Explain the persona, anima/animus, shadow and self archetypes.
Describe Jung's stages of development, the midlife transition and the steps of individuation.
Describe Jung's assessment techniques and the MBTI, and evaluate research findings, contributions and criticisms of his theory.

sections.heading: Analytical Psychology: Jung's Break with Freud
sections.detailed:
Freud once treated Carl Jung as his spiritual son and chosen heir, yet Jung went on to build a personality theory so different from orthodox psychoanalysis that he gave it a new name: analytical psychology. The chapter opens by identifying three main points on which Jung parted company with Freud, and these three points are a favourite exam question.

The first disagreement was about sexuality. Freud treated libido as essentially sexual energy. Jung widened the concept, redefining libido as a general psychic energy of which sex is only one part. Sexuality was not denied, but it lost its position as the master motive of personality.

The second disagreement concerned the direction of the forces that shape us. For Freud, people are largely prisoners of what happened to them in early childhood. Jung rejected this backward-looking determinism. He argued that the future shapes personality as much as the past: we are influenced not only by what we have experienced but also by what we hope and plan to become. This forward-looking, purposive emphasis runs through the whole of his theory, especially in his ideas about the self and individuation.

The third disagreement concerned the unconscious. Most other neo-psychoanalytic dissenters reduced the role of the unconscious, but Jung did the opposite and gave it even more weight than Freud had. He went deeper and added a completely new layer: the inherited experiences of the entire human species and even of pre-human ancestors. Freud had acknowledged inherited primal experiences, but Jung made them the centre of his system, which later appears as the collective unconscious and its archetypes.

To build this picture of human nature Jung drew on history, mythology, anthropology and religion, not just clinical cases. That breadth explains both the richness of analytical psychology and, as the chapter later shows, many of the criticisms made against it.
sections.simple: Jung started as Freud's favourite follower but built his own theory, analytical psychology. He disagreed with Freud on three things: libido is general life energy, not just sex; the future shapes us as much as the past; and the unconscious goes deeper, holding experiences inherited from the whole human species.
keyPoints: Analytical psychology is Jung's name for his theory of personality.
Disagreement 1: libido broadened from sexual energy to general psychic energy.
Disagreement 2: personality is shaped by future goals and aspirations, not only by past events.
Disagreement 3: Jung placed more emphasis on the unconscious than Freud and added inherited species experience.
Jung drew on history, mythology, anthropology and religion to build his theory.

sections.heading: The Life of Jung (1875-1961)
sections.detailed:
The chapter stresses that Jung's theory, like Freud's, was deeply autobiographical, so the life story is not just background but helps explain the theory.

An unhappy childhood. Jung was born in Switzerland into a family with nine clergymen, including his father and eight uncles, so religion and the classics were part of his early world. His father was kind but moody and weak, failing to provide the strong authority Jung wanted. His mother was the more powerful parent but emotionally unstable, switching suddenly from cheerfulness to incoherent mumbling; the boy came to see her as two people in one body. This left him wary of women for many years and may explain why he rejected Freud's claim that every boy sexually desires his mother. To escape his parents' failing marriage he spent hours alone in the attic with a wooden doll he had carved and in which he confided. A sister born when he was nine did not relieve his loneliness.

Dreams and fantasies. Cut off from conscious reality, Jung turned inward to dreams, visions and fantasies, and he continued to look to them for answers throughout life. At three he dreamed of being in a cavern; later he dreamed of digging below the earth and finding bones of prehistoric animals. He read these dreams as pointing him toward the unconscious that lies beneath behaviour, and he titled his autobiography Memories, Dreams, Reflections (1961). Village children avoided him and he avoided them. The chapter links this solitary childhood to a theory focused on inner growth rather than relationships with others, in contrast to Freud's more interpersonal theory.

Medicine. Jung disliked school. A series of fainting spells kept him out for six months, but when he overheard his father worrying about how the boy would ever earn a living, the spells stopped. He later saw that he had unconsciously arranged the illness to avoid school, a lesson about neurosis that left him ashamed. He studied medicine at the University of Basel and chose psychiatry, then a low-status field, because it suited his interest in dreams, the supernatural and the occult. From 1900 he worked at a Zurich mental hospital under Eugen Bleuler, who coined the term schizophrenia. After marrying a very wealthy heiress he left the hospital, lectured at the University of Zurich and built a private practice.

The years with Freud. Jung was already well known when he met Freud in 1907; their first conversation lasted 13 hours. Freud called him his eldest son and crown prince, and Jung saw Freud as a father figure. The relationship showed Oedipal elements, and the chapter suggests it may have been undermined by an experience at 18, when an older male family friend made homosexual overtures to Jung. In 1909 they travelled together to lecture at Clark University in the United States, and Freud groomed Jung, a non-Jew, to lead the International Psychoanalytic Association. But Jung was not an uncritical disciple, and they broke off the relationship in 1913.

The neurotic episode. That same year, aged 38, Jung began a three-year neurotic crisis. He feared losing touch with reality, resigned his lectureship, considered suicide, yet kept treating patients. He had violent apocalyptic dreams and visions, which he recorded with calligraphy and drawings in The Red Book, kept in a Swiss bank vault and published only in 2009. Like Freud, he resolved the crisis by confronting his unconscious through his dreams and fantasies. He concluded that middle age, not childhood, is the most crucial stage of development, and about two-thirds of his patients were middle-aged people with problems like his own.

Sex life and later years. Although he minimised sex in his theory, Jung had an active, anxiety-free sex life with several affairs, which the chapter contrasts with Freud's troubled attitude to sex. In later life he was famous but behaved oddly: greeting kitchen utensils, hiding cash in books and in jars buried in his garden and then forgetting where. He and his wife were cold and formal with their three daughters. He stayed productive for most of his 86 years, and his ideas reached the English-speaking world largely through the financial support of the Rockefeller, McCormick and Mellon families, who arranged translations of his books.
sections.simple: Jung had a lonely, unhappy childhood with a weak father and an unstable mother, and he escaped into dreams and fantasies. He trained in psychiatry, became Freud's chosen heir, then broke with him in 1913 and went through a three-year breakdown. Working through that midlife crisis shaped his theory, especially his belief that middle age is the key period of development.
keyPoints: Lonely childhood with a weak father and unstable mother; turned inward to dreams, which later guided his theory.
Trained in medicine at Basel; worked under Eugen Bleuler in Zurich from 1900.
Met Freud in 1907, travelled with him to Clark University in 1909, broke with him in 1913.
Three-year neurotic episode from age 38; visions recorded in The Red Book (published 2009).
His own midlife crisis led him to see middle age as the most crucial stage of development.
His solitary childhood is reflected in a theory centred on inner growth rather than relationships.

sections.heading: Psychic Energy: The Basis of Jung's System
sections.detailed:
Jung's first major disagreement with Freud was over libido. Jung did not see libido as primarily sexual; he regarded it as a broad, undifferentiated life energy. He actually used the word in two senses. In the wider sense libido is a diffuse, general life energy. In the narrower sense, closer to Freud's usage, it is the psychic energy that fuels the work of the personality, which Jung called the psyche. All psychological activity, such as perceiving, thinking, feeling and wishing, is carried out through this psychic energy.

When a person invests a large amount of psychic energy in a particular idea or feeling, that idea has a high psychic value and can strongly steer the person's life. The chapter's example is someone strongly driven to gain power, who will pour most of their psychic energy into finding ways to get it.

Principles of psychic energy. Borrowing from physics, Jung (1928) proposed three principles that describe how psychic energy works.

1. Principle of opposites. Just as the physical universe contains polarities such as hot and cold, height and depth, or creation and decay, every wish or feeling in the psyche has its opposite. The conflict between these polarities is the main motivator of behaviour and the generator of psychic energy. The sharper the conflict between opposites, the more energy is produced. This principle appears throughout Jung's system, for example in introversion versus extraversion, thinking versus feeling, and conscious versus unconscious.

2. Principle of equivalence. This applies the physical law of conservation of energy to the mind. Energy used to bring about some condition is never lost; it is shifted to another part of the personality. If interest in a person, hobby or subject fades, the energy that was invested in it moves to something new. Energy used for conscious activities while awake moves into dreams during sleep. The word equivalence implies that the new area should have equal psychic value, meaning it should be equally desirable or fascinating; if no such area is found, the surplus energy flows into the unconscious. Either way, energy is continually redistributed within the personality.

3. Principle of entropy. In physics, entropy means that energy differences even out: when a hot and a cold object touch, heat flows from the hotter to the colder until both reach the same temperature. Jung applied this to the psyche as a tendency toward balance or equilibrium. If two desires or beliefs differ greatly in psychic value, energy flows from the stronger to the weaker. The ideal would be an equal spread of energy over all parts of the personality, but this is never reached. In fact, if perfect balance were achieved the personality would have no psychic energy at all, because the principle of opposites says energy is produced only by conflict.

Taken together, the three principles describe a dynamic psyche: opposites generate energy, equivalence keeps it from being lost, and entropy pushes it toward a balance that can be approached but never fully attained. This idea of balancing opposites returns later in the self archetype and in individuation.
sections.simple: Jung saw libido as general life energy, not just sexual energy, and called the personality the psyche. Psychic energy follows three rules borrowed from physics: conflict between opposites creates energy (opposites), energy is never lost but moves elsewhere (equivalence), and energy tends to even out toward balance (entropy).
keyPoints: Libido has two meanings for Jung: general life energy and the narrower psychic energy that runs the psyche.
Psychic value = the amount of energy invested in an idea or feeling.
Opposites: conflict between polarities generates energy; sharper conflict, more energy.
Equivalence: energy is conserved and shifted to an area of equal value, or into the unconscious.
Entropy: energy flows from stronger to weaker values, tending toward a balance that is never fully achieved.

sections.heading: Aspects of Personality: The Ego
sections.detailed:
Jung held that the total personality, the psyche, is made up of several separate systems or aspects that can influence one another. These are the ego, the attitudes and functions that shape conscious experience, the personal unconscious with its complexes, and the collective unconscious with its archetypes.

The ego is the centre of consciousness. It is the part of the psyche concerned with perceiving, thinking, feeling and remembering. It amounts to our awareness of ourselves and is responsible for the ordinary activities of waking life.

An important feature of the ego is that it is selective. Out of the huge number of stimuli we are exposed to, it admits only a portion into conscious awareness. Material that the ego does not admit, or that slips out of awareness, ends up in the personal unconscious, and there is constant traffic between the ego and that layer.

For exam answers, note the contrast with Freud. Jung's ego is simply the conscious aspect of personality, the conscious part of a much larger psyche, most of which is unconscious. It is not the centre of the whole personality: in Jung's scheme that role eventually belongs to the self archetype, which at middle age shifts the centre of personality away from the ego to a point midway between conscious and unconscious.
sections.simple: For Jung the psyche has several parts that interact. The ego is the conscious part: it perceives, thinks, feels and remembers, gives us self-awareness, and lets only some of what we experience into consciousness.
keyPoints: The psyche consists of distinct systems that influence one another.
The ego is the centre of consciousness and of self-awareness.
It handles perceiving, thinking, feeling and remembering in everyday waking life.
It is selective, admitting only part of incoming stimuli into awareness.
Later in life the self archetype shifts the centre of personality away from the ego.

sections.heading: The Attitudes: Extraversion and Introversion
sections.detailed:
A large part of how we consciously perceive and react to our environment depends on two opposing mental attitudes: extraversion and introversion. These are probably Jung's most widely known ideas.

Jung explained the attitudes in terms of the direction in which psychic energy (libido) is channelled. In extraversion, energy is directed outward, toward the external world and other people. Extraverts are described as open, sociable and socially assertive. In introversion, energy is directed inward, toward the self. Introverts are withdrawn, often shy, and focused on their own thoughts and feelings.

Everyone has the capacity for both attitudes, but only one becomes dominant in a given personality. The dominant attitude then directs the person's behaviour and consciousness. Following the principle of opposites, the non-dominant attitude does not disappear. It becomes part of the personal unconscious and can still influence behaviour. The chapter's example is an introvert who, in some situations, behaves in an extraverted way, wishes to be more outgoing, or is attracted to an extravert.

The attitudes are only half of Jung's typology. He noticed that there are different kinds of extraverts and introverts, which led him to add the four psychological functions. Combining the two attitudes with the four functions produces the eight psychological types. The attitudes also matter for development: in young adulthood the dominant conscious attitude is usually extraversion, and at midlife Jung expected a shift toward introversion.

The introversion-extraversion dimension is also one of Jung's lasting contributions; the chapter notes that it is widely accepted, that scales measuring it are standard diagnostic and selection tools, and that most MBTI research has focused on it.
sections.simple: Extraversion means psychic energy is turned outward to people and the world; introversion means it is turned inward to one's own thoughts and feelings. Everyone has both, but one dominates, while the other stays in the personal unconscious and still affects behaviour.
keyPoints: Extraversion: energy directed outward; open, sociable, assertive.
Introversion: energy directed inward; withdrawn, often shy, focused on own thoughts and feelings.
Everyone has both attitudes but only one is dominant.
The non-dominant attitude sits in the personal unconscious and can still influence behaviour.
Attitudes combine with functions to form the eight psychological types.

sections.heading: Psychological Functions
sections.detailed:
Because Jung saw that extraverts and introverts were not all alike, he proposed a further set of distinctions, the psychological functions (Jung, 1927). These are different and opposing ways of perceiving both the external real world and our inner subjective world. There are four: sensing, intuiting, thinking and feeling.

The nonrational functions: sensing and intuiting. These are grouped together as nonrational because they do not use reasoning. They simply take in experience without evaluating it. Sensing reproduces an experience through the senses, much as a photograph copies an object. Intuiting does not come directly from an external stimulus; it works through hunches. The chapter's example is sensing that someone else is in a dark room, not because we saw or heard them but because of a feeling or hunch.

The rational functions: thinking and feeling. These are called rational because they involve making judgments and evaluations about experience. Although they are opposites, both organise and categorise experience. Thinking makes a conscious judgment about whether an experience is true or false. Feeling evaluates experience in terms of like or dislike, pleasant or unpleasant, stimulating or dull. Note that for Jung feeling is a rational function: it is a way of judging, not merely an emotion.

Dominance. Just as everyone has both attitudes, everyone has the capacity for all four functions. But only one function is dominant; the others are submerged in the personal unconscious. Further, only one pair is dominant, either the rational pair or the nonrational pair, and within that pair only one function rules. A person cannot be governed by both thinking and feeling, or by both sensing and intuiting, because each pair consists of opposites. This is the principle of opposites at work again.

Exam tip: the chapter's review questions ask why thinking and feeling are rational while sensing and intuiting are nonrational. The answer is that the first pair judges and evaluates experience, whereas the second pair only receives or perceives it without evaluation.
sections.simple: Jung named four functions: sensing and intuiting, which take in experience without judging it (nonrational), and thinking and feeling, which judge experience (rational). We have all four, but only one is dominant and the rest sit in the personal unconscious.
keyPoints: Four functions: sensing, intuiting, thinking, feeling.
Sensing and intuiting are nonrational: they accept experience without evaluating it.
Sensing works like a photograph of the senses; intuiting works through hunches.
Thinking (true/false) and feeling (like/dislike) are rational: they judge and evaluate.
Only one function is dominant; opposing functions cannot both rule.

sections.heading: Psychological Types
sections.detailed:
By crossing the two attitudes with the four functions, Jung proposed eight psychological types (Table 3.1 in the book). Each type is described by its dominant attitude and dominant function.

Extraverted thinking types live strictly by society's rules. They repress feelings and emotions, try to be objective in every area of life, and can be dogmatic in their opinions, so others may see them as rigid and cold. Their focus on understanding the external world through logical rules makes them good scientists.

Extraverted feeling types repress thinking and are highly emotional. They conform to the traditional values and moral codes they were taught, are very sensitive to others' opinions and expectations, make friends easily, and are sociable and lively. Jung thought this type was more common among women than men.

Extraverted sensing types seek pleasure, happiness and new experiences. They are strongly oriented to the real world, adapt easily to different people and changing situations, are not introspective, and have a great capacity for enjoying life.

Extraverted intuiting types succeed in business and politics because they are good at spotting and exploiting opportunities. They like new ideas, are creative and can inspire others to achieve. They are changeable, moving from one venture to another, and decide on hunches rather than reflection, though their decisions tend to be right.

Introverted thinking types do not get along well with others and find it hard to communicate their ideas. They focus on thoughts rather than feelings, have poor practical judgment, value privacy, prefer abstractions and theories, and try to understand themselves rather than other people. Others see them as stubborn, aloof, arrogant and inconsiderate.

Introverted feeling types repress rational thought. They are capable of deep emotion but avoid expressing it outwardly, so they seem mysterious, quiet, modest and childish. They show little consideration for others' feelings and appear withdrawn, cold and self-assured.

Introverted sensing types seem passive, calm and detached from everyday life, viewing human activity with benevolence and amusement. They are aesthetically sensitive, expressing themselves through art or music, and repress intuition.

Introverted intuiting types are so absorbed in intuition that they have little contact with reality. They are visionaries and daydreamers, aloof, impractical and poorly understood, often seen as odd and eccentric, and they struggle with everyday life and planning for the future.

The typology later inspired the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator. The chapter also notes that, according to Jung, people are classifiable into types mainly in the first half of life; after progress toward individuation at midlife, no single aspect dominates and the person can no longer be described as one particular type.
sections.simple: Combining two attitudes (extraversion, introversion) with four functions (thinking, feeling, sensing, intuiting) gives Jung's eight personality types, such as the logical extraverted thinker or the dreamy introverted intuitive. These types later became the basis of the MBTI.
keyPoints: Eight types = 2 attitudes x 4 functions.
Extraverted thinking: logical, objective, dogmatic; good scientists.
Extraverted feeling: emotional, sociable, sensitive to others; Jung thought more common in women.
Extraverted sensing: pleasure-seeking, adaptable; extraverted intuiting: creative, opportunity-seizing.
Introverted thinking: ideas over people; introverted feeling: deep but hidden emotion.
Introverted sensing: detached, aesthetic; introverted intuiting: visionary, out of touch with reality.

sections.heading: The Personal Unconscious and Complexes
sections.detailed:
The personal unconscious. In Jung's system the personal unconscious resembles Freud's preconscious. It is a reservoir of material that was once conscious but has been forgotten or suppressed, either because it was trivial or because it was disturbing. There is a great deal of two-way traffic between the ego and the personal unconscious; for instance, attention can drift from what you are reading to a memory of something you did yesterday, and then return. The personal unconscious has been compared to a filing cabinet: little effort is needed to take a memory out, look at it, and put it back until it is needed again. It is also where the non-dominant attitude and the three non-dominant functions reside.

Complexes. As more experiences are filed in the personal unconscious, they become grouped into complexes. A complex is a core or pattern of emotions, memories, perceptions and wishes organised around a common theme. Someone with a complex about power or status is preoccupied with that theme to the point that it shapes their behaviour; they might run for elected office, or try to identify with power by driving a motorcycle or a fast car. By directing thought and behaviour, the complex determines how the person sees the world.

Complexes can be conscious or unconscious. Those outside conscious control can intrude on and interfere with consciousness. Typically the person with the complex is unaware of its influence, even though other people can easily see its effects.

Complexes are not always harmful. Some can be useful: a perfection or achievement complex may drive a person to work hard at developing talents or skills. This is a point of difference from the purely pathological way the word is often used.

Origins. Jung believed complexes arise not only from childhood and adult experience but also from ancestral experience, the heritage of the species stored in the collective unconscious. This links the personal layer of the unconscious to the deeper collective layer.

Complexes also connect to assessment: Jung's word-association test was designed precisely to uncover complexes, using signs such as delayed responses or physiological reactions to particular stimulus words. The concept of the complex is listed among Jung's lasting contributions to psychology.
sections.simple: The personal unconscious holds things we once knew but forgot or pushed away, and we can easily pull them back, like files from a cabinet. Over time these memories cluster into complexes, emotional patterns around a theme like power, which can quietly steer behaviour and may be harmful or helpful.
keyPoints: Personal unconscious: once-conscious material that was forgotten or suppressed; similar to Freud's preconscious.
Constant two-way traffic with the ego; likened to a filing cabinet.
Complex: a pattern of emotions, memories, perceptions and wishes around a common theme.
Complexes may be conscious or unconscious; the person is often unaware of their influence.
Complexes can be useful (achievement complex) as well as harmful.
Complexes arise from childhood, adult and ancestral experience.

sections.heading: The Collective Unconscious
sections.detailed:
The collective unconscious is the deepest and least accessible level of the psyche and the most unusual and controversial part of Jung's theory. Just as each individual stores personal experiences in the personal unconscious, humankind as a species stores the experiences of all its human and pre-human ancestors in the collective unconscious, and this heritage passes to each new generation.

Jung held that experiences which are universal, repeated in every generation, become part of our personality. Our primitive past thus forms the basis of the human psyche and directs present behaviour. In this way Jung linked each person's personality not just to childhood but to the history of the species.

What is inherited is a predisposition, not the experience itself. We do not inherit a fear of snakes; we inherit the potential to fear snakes. We are predisposed to feel and behave as people always have, but whether a predisposition becomes reality depends on the experiences we actually encounter.

Certain basic experiences have marked every generation: having a mother figure, birth and death, facing unknown terrors in the dark, worshipping power or a godlike figure, and fearing an evil being. Their universality over countless generations leaves an imprint on each of us at birth that shapes how we perceive and respond to the world. For example, a baby is born predisposed to perceive its mother in a certain way; if the mother behaves as mothers typically do, nurturing and supporting, the baby's inborn expectation matches reality.

Evidence Jung offered. Because the idea is so unusual, the chapter explains why Jung proposed it. First, in studying ancient cultures, both mythical and real, he found common themes and symbols in widely separated parts of the world which, as far as he could tell, had not been passed between cultures by speech or writing. Second, his patients described in their dreams and fantasies the same kinds of symbols he had found in ancient cultures. He could think of no other explanation for shared symbols across such vast distances of space and time than that they are carried in every person's unconscious mind.

Critically, this evidence comes from mythology, religion and patients' reports rather than controlled observation, which is one reason the collective unconscious is regarded as controversial and difficult to test scientifically.
sections.simple: The collective unconscious is the deepest layer of the mind, holding experiences inherited from all our human and pre-human ancestors. We do not inherit actual memories but tendencies, like the potential to fear snakes. Jung based the idea on similar symbols appearing in ancient myths and in his patients' dreams across the world.
keyPoints: Deepest, least accessible and most controversial level of the psyche.
Stores inherited experiences of human and pre-human ancestors; passed to each generation.
We inherit predispositions (e.g., potential to fear snakes), not the experiences themselves.
Universal experiences: mother figure, birth, death, darkness, power, evil.
Evidence: common symbols in unconnected ancient cultures and in patients' dreams and fantasies.

sections.heading: Archetypes
sections.detailed:
The ancient experiences stored in the collective unconscious show themselves as recurring themes or patterns, which Jung called archetypes (Jung, 1947). He also called them primordial images. In the book's definition, archetypes are images of universal experiences contained in the collective unconscious.

There are as many archetypes as there are common human experiences. Because they have been repeated in the lives of generation after generation, they have become imprinted on our psyches, and they are expressed in our dreams and fantasies.

Examples Jung proposed include the hero, the mother, the child, God, death, power and the wise old man. A few archetypes are developed more fully than the rest and influence the psyche more consistently. These major archetypes are:

1. the persona, the public mask;
2. the anima and animus, the opposite-sex aspects of the psyche;
3. the shadow, the dark, primitive side of personality; and
4. the self, the archetype of unity and wholeness.

Each of these is treated in its own section below. Together they show how the principle of opposites works at the deepest level: persona versus true self, masculine versus feminine, civilised versus animal, and conscious versus unconscious. In middle age, during individuation, the person must come to terms with each major archetype in turn: dethroning the persona, accepting the shadow, accepting the anima or animus, and finally moving toward the self through transcendence.

Archetypes also matter for research: Cann and Donderi (1986) studied whether archetypal content appears in people's dreams and whether this varies with personality type.
sections.simple: Archetypes are inherited images of universal human experiences, such as the hero, mother or wise old man, that show up in dreams and fantasies. The four most important are the persona, the anima/animus, the shadow and the self.
keyPoints: Archetypes (primordial images) express the contents of the collective unconscious.
They are imprinted through repetition across generations and appear in dreams and fantasies.
Examples: hero, mother, child, God, death, power, wise old man.
Major archetypes: persona, anima and animus, shadow, self.
Individuation involves coming to terms with each major archetype.

sections.heading: The Persona
sections.detailed:
The word persona originally meant the mask an actor wore to show different roles or faces to an audience, and Jung used it in much the same sense. The persona archetype is a mask or public face that we wear to present ourselves as someone different from who we really are.

Jung thought the persona was necessary. We are required to play many roles in life to succeed at school and work and to get along with a wide variety of people. A suitable public face makes this possible.

The danger arises when we start to believe the mask is our true nature. Instead of merely playing a role, we become it. Other aspects of the personality are then blocked from developing. When the ego identifies with the persona rather than with the person's real nature, the result is a condition Jung called inflation of the persona.

Jung saw deception in both cases. A person who plays a role is deceiving others; a person who comes to believe in the role is deceiving himself or herself.

The persona also features in individuation. At midlife the first change in the archetypes is dethroning the persona: we must keep playing social roles in order to function, but recognise that our public personality may not reflect our true nature and accept the genuine self the persona has been hiding. In the first half of life the persona also serves to hide the shadow, both from others and from ourselves.

A review question in the chapter asks students to distinguish the persona from the self archetype: the persona is a surface mask oriented to social demands, whereas the self is the deep archetype of unity and wholeness of the entire personality.
sections.simple: The persona is the social mask we show the world so we can fit our many roles. It is useful, but if we start believing the mask is the real us, other parts of personality cannot grow, which Jung called inflation of the persona.
keyPoints: Persona = the public face or role presented to others, like an actor's mask.
Necessary for functioning in school, work and varied social settings.
Harmful if we believe it is our true nature.
Inflation of the persona: the ego identifies with the persona instead of the true self.
Playing a role deceives others; believing it deceives oneself.
At midlife the persona must be dethroned.

sections.heading: The Anima and Animus
sections.detailed:
The anima and animus archetypes express Jung's view that human beings are essentially bisexual. At the biological level, each sex secretes the hormones of the other sex as well as its own. At the psychological level, each sex shows characteristics, temperaments and attitudes of the other sex, acquired through centuries of living together.

The anima is the feminine aspect of the male psyche. The animus is the masculine aspect of the female psyche. The book illustrates this with the yin-yang symbol (Figure 3.1), where each half contains a dot of the opposite colour to show that each side expresses some characteristics of its opposite.

Function. These opposite-sex characteristics help the adjustment and survival of the species because they allow members of one sex to understand the nature of the other. The archetypes predispose us to like certain qualities in the opposite sex and guide our behaviour toward the opposite sex.

Must be expressed. Jung insisted that both the anima and the animus must be expressed. A man must show his feminine characteristics alongside his masculine ones, and a woman must express her masculine characteristics along with her feminine ones. If these aspects are not expressed, they remain dormant and undeveloped, and the personality becomes one-sided. So the answer to the chapter's review question, whether the anima and animus should be suppressed or expressed, is clearly that they should be expressed.

In individuation. At midlife a man must express his anima, traditionally feminine traits such as tenderness, and a woman must express her animus, traditionally masculine traits such as assertiveness. Jung considered this the most difficult step in individuation because it involves the greatest change in self-image. Accepting the emotional qualities of both sexes opens new sources of creativity and serves as the final release from parental influences.
sections.simple: Jung believed everyone is psychologically part male and part female. The anima is the feminine side in men and the animus is the masculine side in women. Both must be expressed; otherwise the personality becomes one-sided.
keyPoints: Based on Jung's view that humans are essentially bisexual, biologically and psychologically.
Anima: feminine aspects of the male psyche; animus: masculine aspects of the female psyche.
They help each sex understand the other and guide behaviour toward the opposite sex.
Both must be expressed to avoid a one-sided personality.
Accepting them is the hardest step in individuation.

sections.heading: The Shadow
sections.detailed:
The shadow is the most powerful archetype and has the deepest roots of all, because it contains the basic, primitive animal instincts. Behaviours that society regards as evil and immoral reside in the shadow. This dark side of human nature has to be tamed if people are to live together in harmony: we must constantly restrain, overcome and defend against these primitive impulses, or society is likely to punish us.

The dilemma. The shadow is not only the source of evil. It is also the source of vitality, spontaneity, creativity and emotion. If the shadow is completely suppressed, the psyche becomes dull and lifeless. The ego's job is therefore a balancing act: to repress the animal instincts enough for us to be considered civilised, while allowing enough of them to be expressed to provide creativity and vigour.

The danger of total suppression. Complete suppression has a second risk beyond a flat personality. The instincts do not vanish when suppressed; they lie dormant, waiting for a crisis or a weakness in the ego. When that happens they may revolt and take control, leaving the person dominated by the unconscious.

In individuation. At midlife we must accept our dark side. We become aware of the shadow's destructive forces and acknowledge primitive impulses such as selfishness, without submitting to them. In the first half of life the persona shields the shadow from others, and in hiding it from others we also hide it from ourselves. Greater awareness of both the destructive and constructive sides of the shadow gives the personality a deeper and fuller dimension, since its tendencies bring zest and spontaneity to life.

Human nature. The shadow is also the source of the spontaneity that leaves room for free will in Jung's system.

Comparison with Freud. The chapter's review questions ask how the shadow compares with Freud's id. On the basis of this chapter, both contain primitive animal instincts and impulses society condemns. The difference is that Jung's shadow is an inherited archetype of the collective unconscious that is also a source of creativity and vitality, and it should be partly expressed and consciously accepted rather than only controlled.
sections.simple: The shadow is the dark, animal side of personality and the most powerful archetype. It holds impulses society sees as evil, but also our energy, spontaneity and creativity. So the ego should tame it, not crush it, or life feels flat and the shadow may break out in a crisis.
keyPoints: Most powerful archetype with the deepest roots; contains primitive animal instincts.
Home of behaviour society considers evil and immoral; must be tamed.
Also the source of vitality, spontaneity, creativity and emotion.
Total suppression leaves a dull psyche and risks the shadow revolting in a crisis.
In individuation the shadow must be acknowledged, not obeyed.

sections.heading: The Self
sections.detailed:
The self archetype represents the unity, integration and harmony of the total personality. For Jung, striving toward this wholeness is the ultimate goal of life.

The self involves bringing together and balancing all parts of the personality. Here the principle of opposites reaches its fullest expression. The opposites of conscious and unconscious processes must be assimilated, so that the centre of personality moves from the ego to a point of equilibrium midway between the conscious and the unconscious. As a result, unconscious material gains greater influence on the personality.

A future goal. The full realisation of the self lies in the future. It is something always strived for but rarely achieved. The self is therefore a motivating force that pulls us from ahead, rather than pushing us from behind as past experiences do. This captures Jung's teleological, forward-looking view of personality, in contrast to Freud's emphasis on the past.

Timing. The self cannot begin to emerge until all the other systems of the psyche have developed, which happens around middle age, the crucial transition period in Jung's system and in his own life. Actualising the self requires goals and plans for the future and an accurate perception of one's own abilities.

Difficulty. Because the self cannot develop without self-knowledge, Jung saw it as the most difficult process in life, requiring persistence, perceptiveness and wisdom.

The self is closely tied to individuation and transcendence: individuation is the process of integrating conscious and unconscious aspects, and transcendence is the innate tendency toward unity that completes it. The chapter also notes that Jung's idea of individuation, or self-actualisation, anticipated Abraham Maslow's work.
sections.simple: The self is the archetype of wholeness, the drive to bring every part of the personality into balance. It is a future goal that pulls us forward, usually starts emerging only in middle age, and is rarely fully reached because it requires deep self-knowledge.
keyPoints: Self = unity, integration and harmony of the whole personality; the ultimate goal of life.
The centre of personality shifts from the ego to a point between conscious and unconscious.
A future goal that pulls us forward rather than a past that pushes us.
Emerges only around middle age, after the other systems have developed.
Requires self-knowledge; the most difficult process in life.

sections.heading: The Development of the Personality
sections.detailed:
Jung believed personality is determined by what we hope to become as well as by what we have been and what happened to us in the past. He criticised Freud for stressing only past events. For Jung we grow and develop at every age, always moving toward a more complete level of self-realisation. He took a longer view than Freud, who focused on the first years and expected little development after age 5. Jung did not describe detailed sequential stages, but he wrote of two general periods of development (Jung, 1930). Table 3.2 in the book summarises them as childhood, puberty to young adulthood, and middle age.

Childhood to young adulthood. The ego begins to develop in early childhood, at first in a primitive way because the child has no unique identity yet. A child's personality at this stage is little more than a reflection of the parents' personalities, so parents have great influence: they can help or hinder development by how they behave. Some parents try to impose their own personalities, wanting the child to be an extension of themselves; others expect a very different personality as a way of making up for their own shortcomings. The ego forms substantively only when the child can distinguish between self and other people or objects; consciousness forms when the child can say "I."

The psyche takes on a definite form and content only at puberty, which Jung called psychic birth. This period brings difficulties and the need to adapt, since childhood fantasies must give way to the demands of reality. From the teens through young adulthood we are busy with preparatory activities: finishing education, starting a career, marrying and starting a family. Our focus is external, consciousness is dominant, and our primary conscious attitude is usually extraversion. The aim is to reach our goals and secure a successful place in the world, so young adulthood should be an exciting, challenging time.

Middle age. Jung believed major personality changes occur between 35 and 40. This was the period of his own crisis and that of many of his patients. By about 40, the typical person is established in career, marriage and community, so Jung asked why so many successful people at that age feel despair and worthlessness. His patients reported feeling empty: adventure and excitement were gone and life had lost meaning.

Jung concluded that these changes are inevitable and universal, a natural transition in which the personality is supposed to undergo necessary and beneficial change. Ironically, the change happens because people have been so successful. They invested great energy in the preparatory tasks of the first half of life; by 40 those tasks are done, but the energy remains and has nowhere to go, so (consistent with the principle of equivalence) it must be rechannelled into new activities and interests.

The first half of life is devoted to the objective world of education, career and family; the second half must be devoted to the neglected inner, subjective world. The attitude must shift from extraversion to introversion, consciousness must be balanced by awareness of the unconscious, and interests must move from the physical and material to the spiritual, philosophical and intuitive. A balance among all parts of personality must replace the earlier exclusive focus on consciousness. In this way middle age begins the process of realising the self, and if conscious and unconscious are successfully integrated, a person can reach the new level of psychological health Jung called individuation.
sections.simple: Jung said personality keeps developing throughout life and is shaped by future goals, not just the past. The first half of life (up to young adulthood) is outward-focused on education, career and family; puberty is our 'psychic birth'. Around 35-40, energy must turn inward toward the unconscious and spiritual concerns, opening the path to individuation.
keyPoints: Personality is shaped by future hopes as well as past experience; development continues through life.
Childhood: personality mirrors the parents; ego forms when the child can distinguish self from others.
Puberty = psychic birth, when the psyche gains definite form and content.
Young adulthood: external focus, conscious dominant, extraversion; preparatory activities.
Middle age (35-40): major, universal and beneficial change; energy redirected inward.
Shift from extraversion to introversion and from material to spiritual interests.

sections.heading: Individuation: How to Reach Fulfillment
sections.detailed:
Individuation means becoming an individual, fulfilling one's capacities and developing one's self. The book defines it as a condition of psychological health resulting from the integration of all conscious and unconscious facets of personality. The tendency toward individuation is innate and inevitable, but environmental forces can help or hinder it, including educational and economic opportunities and the nature of the parent-child relationship. Jung described several steps on the way to this ideal.

1. Confront the unconscious. Middle-aged people must abandon the behaviours and values that guided the first half of life and confront their unconscious, bringing it into awareness and accepting what it tells them. They must listen to their dreams, follow their fantasies, and use creative imagination through writing, painting or other forms of expression. They should be guided not by the rational thinking that drove them earlier but by the spontaneous flow of the unconscious, because only then can the true self appear. Jung cautioned that admitting unconscious forces does not mean being dominated by them; they must be assimilated and balanced with the conscious. In a healthy middle-aged person no single aspect dominates: not consciousness or unconsciousness, not any one attitude or function, and not any archetype.

2. Dethrone the persona. The first change in the archetypes is dethroning the persona. We still have to play social roles to function, but we must recognise that our public personality may not represent our true nature and accept the genuine self the persona has been covering.

3. Accept our dark sides. Next we become aware of the shadow's destructive forces and acknowledge primitive impulses such as selfishness, without submitting to them. In the first half of life the persona shields the shadow, and hiding it from others also hides it from ourselves. Awareness of both the destructive and constructive sides of the shadow adds depth and brings zest, spontaneity and vitality. Knowing only our good side produces one-sided development; both sides must be expressed.

4. Accept our anima and animus. We must come to terms with our psychological bisexuality: a man expressing traditionally feminine traits such as tenderness, and a woman expressing traditionally masculine traits such as assertiveness. Jung considered this the most difficult step because it means the biggest change in self-image. It opens new sources of creativity and serves as the final release from parental influences.

5. Transcend. Once the psyche's structures are individuated and acknowledged, transcendence can occur. Transcendence is an innate tendency toward unity or wholeness, uniting all the opposing aspects of the psyche. Environmental factors such as an unsatisfactory marriage or a frustrating job can block transcendence and prevent full achievement of the self.

The central theme throughout is harmony: each aspect of personality must be brought into balance with every other. Research reported in the chapter, such as Lyons's (2002) study of senior executives and studies of women at midlife, found behaviour consistent with this description of individuation.
sections.simple: Individuation is becoming your full, integrated self by bringing conscious and unconscious into balance, usually from middle age. The steps are: face your unconscious, drop the illusion that your social mask is you, accept your dark side, accept your opposite-sex side, and finally transcend toward wholeness.
keyPoints: Individuation = integrating all conscious and unconscious facets; innate but can be helped or hindered.
Step 1: confront the unconscious through dreams, fantasies and creative expression, without being ruled by it.
Step 2: dethrone the persona.
Step 3: accept the shadow's existence without submitting to it.
Step 4: accept anima/animus; the hardest step.
Step 5: transcendence, the innate tendency toward unity, which bad marriages or jobs can block.

sections.heading: Questions about Human Nature
sections.detailed:
Jung's image of human nature differs substantially from Freud's. The main dimensions can be summarised as follows.

Free will versus determinism. Jung's view was less deterministic than Freud's. He agreed that personality may be partly determined by childhood experiences and by the archetypes, but his system leaves ample room for free will and spontaneity, the latter coming from the shadow archetype.

Nature versus nurture. Jung took a mixed position. The drive toward individuation and transcendence is innate, but learning and experience can help or block it.

Ultimate goal. The ultimate and necessary goal of life is realisation of the self. It is rarely achieved, but we are continually motivated to strive for it.

Importance of childhood. Jung disagreed with Freud here. Childhood experiences matter but do not fully shape personality by age 5. We are affected more by our experiences in middle age and by our hopes and expectations for the future.

Uniqueness versus universality. Each person is unique, but only in the first half of life. When some progress toward individuation is made in middle age, a universal kind of personality develops in which no single aspect dominates. Uniqueness then disappears, and we can no longer be described as one particular psychological type.

Optimism. Jung's image was more positive and hopeful than Freud's. We are motivated to grow, improve and extend ourselves, and development continues throughout life rather than stopping in childhood. Jung also believed the human species keeps improving, with present generations a significant advance over primitive ancestors.

A watchful optimism. Despite this, Jung warned of a danger to Western culture that he called a sickness of dissociation. By overemphasising materialism, reason and empirical science, people risk failing to appreciate the forces of the unconscious and abandoning trust in the archetypes that form our heritage. His hopefulness was therefore a warning kind of optimism.
sections.simple: Compared with Freud, Jung was more optimistic and less deterministic: people have free will, keep growing throughout life, and are pulled by future goals. Personality is part inborn and part learned, and uniqueness fades after midlife individuation. He warned that the West overvalues materialism and science and neglects the unconscious.
keyPoints: Less deterministic than Freud; room for free will and spontaneity (from the shadow).
Nature-nurture: mixed; drive to individuation is innate but shaped by experience.
Childhood matters, but midlife experience and future hopes matter more.
Uniqueness only in the first half of life; a universal personality emerges after individuation.
Optimistic about individuals and the species, but warned of a 'sickness of dissociation' in Western culture.

sections.heading: Assessment in Jung's Theory
sections.detailed:
Jung's assessment methods combined science and the supernatural, producing both an objective and a mystical approach. He investigated many cultures and eras, studying their symbols, myths, religions and rituals, and formed his theory from his patients' fantasies and dreams (and his own) together with explorations of ancient languages, alchemy and astrology. Yet what first brought him to the attention of American psychologists was empirical and physiological work, so his methods were an unusual blend of opposites, fitting a theory built on the principle of opposites.

Jung's sessions with patients. His sessions were unconventional and often chaotic. Patients did not lie on a couch; Jung and the patient usually sat facing each other in comfortable chairs, sometimes with Jung looking out at the lake, and occasionally he took patients out on his sailboat. A patient recalled him pacing and gesturing, then suddenly sitting very close to deliver a pointed interpretation. He could be rude, sending one patient home to cure herself, and cutting short a patient who wanted to talk about her mother, a topic Freud would have encouraged. He accepted patients' fantasies as real for them; he told Marie-Louise von Franz, later his lifelong disciple, about a patient who truly lived on the moon.

Word association. In this test the subject responds to a stimulus word with whatever word first comes to mind; it became a standard laboratory and clinical tool. In the early 1900s Jung used a list of 100 emotionally evocative words, measured response time, and recorded physiological reactions. He used it to uncover complexes. Signs of a complex included physiological responses, delays, giving the same response to different words, slips of the tongue, stammering, answering with more than one word, inventing words, or failing to respond. Table 3.3 contrasts normal and neurotic responses.

Symptom analysis. This focuses on the symptoms the patient reports and on the patient's free associations to them. It is similar to Freud's cathartic method. Through the patient's associations and the analyst's interpretations, symptoms are often relieved or disappear.

Dream analysis. Jung agreed with Freud that dreams are the royal road to the unconscious, but he was concerned with more than their causes and saw them as more than unconscious wishes. Dreams are prospective: they help us prepare for experiences we expect. They are also compensatory: they restore balance between opposites by compensating for the overdevelopment of any one psychic structure. Instead of interpreting single dreams as Freud did, Jung worked with a series of dreams over time to find recurring themes. He also used amplification: rather than following a chain of free associations away from a dream element, he kept the patient returning to the original element and making repeated associations until a theme emerged. He did not distinguish manifest from latent content.

The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator. The MBTI, developed by Katharine Cook Briggs and Isabel Briggs Myers, assesses Jung's psychological types and attitudes. It is described as the most popular personality test ever devised, taken by over two million people a year for hiring and promotion decisions. Katharine was struck by the personality differences between her intuitive daughter Isabel and Isabel's practical, logical fiancé Clarence Myers. After reading Jung's Psychological Types in 1923, she found a way to classify such differences and, with Isabel and without grants or university support, built a test. In 1975 Isabel Briggs Myers and Mary McCaulley founded the Center for Applications of Psychological Type, and the Association for Psychological Type followed in 1979. The MBTI is considered the most visible practical outgrowth of Jung's work.
sections.simple: Jung assessed personality through a mix of science and mysticism, studying myths and symbols as well as patients. His formal methods were the word-association test (to find complexes), symptom analysis (free association to symptoms) and dream analysis (series of dreams, amplification; dreams as prospective and compensatory). The MBTI was later built by Briggs and Myers to measure his types.
keyPoints: Blend of objective and mystical methods: myths, symbols, alchemy, astrology plus physiological measures.
Unconventional sessions: face to face, no couch, sometimes on his sailboat.
Word association: 100 words, reaction time and physiological responses used to detect complexes.
Symptom analysis: free associations to symptoms; similar to Freud's cathartic method.
Dream analysis: dreams are prospective and compensatory; dream series and amplification.
MBTI: by Briggs and Myers; most popular personality test, used in hiring and promotion.

sections.heading: Research on Jung's Theory: Methods and Psychological Types
sections.detailed:
Jung's method. Like Freud, Jung used the case study method, which he called life-history reconstruction: an extensive recollection of a person's past experiences to identify the developmental patterns that led to the present neurotic condition.

Criticisms of his data. The criticisms of Freud's methods apply to Jung too. His data were not based on objective observation and were not gathered in a controlled, systematic way. Clinical interviews could not be duplicated, verified or quantified. He kept no verbatim records and did not check the accuracy of patients' reports. His cases were a small, unrepresentative sample, which limits generalisation. His analysis was subjective and unreliable; he never explained his procedures and interpreted data in light of his studies of cultures and his own dreams and fantasies. He has been accused of slanting conclusions to fit his theory, and it is alleged that his midlife visions can be traced to material he had read (Noll). Many of his observations cannot be tested experimentally, and Jung was indifferent to this, remarking that experimental psychology could teach almost nothing about the human mind.

Research on psychological types. Despite this, some aspects of the theory have been tested, with results supporting some of Jung's propositions. Most of this research uses the MBTI and focuses on introversion and extraversion, though not all studies support Jung's types (Pittenger, 2005).

Studies of college students and occupations. Stricker and Ross (1962) found that job interests matched Jungian attitudes and types: introverts preferred work with little personal interaction, such as technical and scientific jobs, while extraverts preferred highly social jobs like sales and public relations. Introverted feeling and judging types had higher grade point averages (DiRienzo et al., 2010). Hanewitz (1978) found teachers and social work students high in intuiting and feeling, while police officers and dental students were high in extraversion, sensing and thinking. Students high in intuiting had more creative vocational interests and those high in sensing more conventional ones (Apostal, 1991). Among women at the U.S. Naval Academy, extraverted-sensing-thinking-judging types were most likely to graduate and those high in feeling and perceiving most likely to drop out (Murray & Johnson, 2001); a 10-year study at liberal arts colleges also linked perceiving to dropping out (Barrineau, 2005). Medical students who became primary care physicians were high in feeling and introversion, while future surgeons were extraverted thinking types (Stilwell et al., 2000). Extraverts scored higher than introverts on psychological well-being and life satisfaction (Harrington & Loffredo, 2001).

Studies of cognitive functioning. Introverted thinking types remember neutral, impersonal stimuli such as numbers better, while extraverted feeling types remember emotional human stimuli such as facial expressions better (Carlson & Levy, 1973). EEG brain-wave activity differed across MBTI types (Gram, Dunn & Ellis, 2005). When asked to recall vivid emotional experiences, extraverted feeling types recalled memories involving other people and highly emotional details, while introverted thinking types recalled events when they were alone and more neutral, factual experiences (Carlson, 1980).

Studies of diverse cultures. The MBTI has been translated for use in Turkey, Syria and other Arab countries. Among Muslims in England, religious participation was linked to extraversion and thinking (Francis & Datoo, 2012); Greek Orthodox churchgoers in London scored high in introversion, sensing, thinking and judging (Lewis et al., 2012). In Israel, extraverted and feeling women students were happier (Francis, Yablon & Robbins, 2013). In Singapore extraverts preferred face-to-face communication and introverts online contact (Goby, 2006). Bulgarian adolescents high in intuiting and sensing had greater self-esteem (Papazova & Pencheva, 2008). Among junior and mid-level managers in India, those very high in thinking managed conflict collaboratively while those high in feeling avoided conflict; men scored higher on thinking and women on feeling (Mathew & Bhatewara, 2006). In China, no gender differences in MBTI scores were found among managers (Huifang & Shuming, 2004), and Chinese managers' scores were closer to U.S. managers than to the Chinese general population (Yang & Zhao, 2009). For Australians and Canadians, social attention was the key motivator for high extraverts (Ashton, Lee & Paunonen, 2002).
sections.simple: Jung used life-history reconstruction (case studies), which is criticised as unsystematic, unverifiable and subjective. Still, MBTI research supports parts of his typology: introverts and extraverts prefer different jobs, types differ in memory and brain activity, and type differences appear across many cultures, including Indian managers.
keyPoints: Life-history reconstruction: Jung's case study method; shares the weaknesses of Freud's data.
Data were uncontrolled, unverified, unrepresentative and subjectively analysed; many ideas untestable.
Most research uses the MBTI and focuses on introversion-extraversion; support is partial (Pittenger, 2005).
Introverts prefer technical/scientific work; extraverts prefer social jobs (Stricker & Ross, 1962).
Types differ in memory for impersonal vs emotional stimuli and in EEG activity.
Cross-cultural MBTI findings include Indian managers: thinking linked to collaborative conflict management.

sections.heading: Research on Dreams, Individuation and the Midlife Crisis in Women
sections.detailed:
Research on dreams. Cann and Donderi (1986) asked participants to recall their most recent, most vivid and earliest dreams over three weeks and gave them the MBTI and another personality test. Introverts were more likely than extraverts to recall everyday dreams unrelated to archetypes. Intuiting types recalled more archetypal dreams than sensing types. People high in neuroticism recalled fewer archetypal dreams than those low in neuroticism. The researchers concluded that these results agreed with predictions from Jung's theory.

Individuation. Lyons (2002) intensively studied men and women aged 37 to 55 in senior executive positions, using interviews with the executives, their colleagues and families, on-the-job observation, and the TAT, MBTI and Adjective Check List. The executives looked inward for direction and energy, questioned inherited values, shed outdated parts of themselves, revealed new dimensions, became more playful and spontaneous, and acted on their own wishes rather than simply reacting to outside pressures. These characteristics correspond to Jung's description of individuation.

The midlife crisis in women. Jung and others first saw the midlife crisis as far more likely in men, but more recently a similar crisis in women has been recognised. A U.S. national survey found women in worse health than men, feeling little control over their marriages and having fewer job opportunities (Barrett, 2005). Women with more stressful life changes at midlife were less satisfied with life (Darling, Coccia & Senatore, 2012). Lesbian women reported less emotional turmoil at midlife than heterosexual women, and Black women had more positive self-perceptions in middle age than White women. A survey of women in their 50s, studied since their senior year in college, found the early 40s to be the period of greatest conflict (Helson, 1992). Many women undergo intense self-evaluation at midlife; the transition was less difficult for women who had pursued careers than for those focused on marriage and family, many of whom judged their marriages partial or complete failures and considered drastic changes (Levinson, 1996).

Making life changes. Two samples of college-educated women, studied as students and again in their late 30s or early 40s, mostly went through a period of life reevaluation around age 40, as Jung predicted, and about two-thirds made major life changes between 37 and 43 as a result. Asked at 37 whether they would make the same choices again, 34 percent from an affluent private college and 61 percent from a large state university said no; they would have pursued education and careers over family goals. Another sample found that two-thirds believed they had been less successful than their adult daughters who worked outside the home (Carr, 2004). Women who managed satisfying life changes by 43 reported greater well-being, a stronger sense of identity and an enlarged view of their capabilities than those who could not, so regret led to positive change (Stewart & Ostrove, 1998; Stewart & Vandewater, 1999).

Personal growth or stagnation? A 20-year longitudinal study of women after college (John, Pals & Westenberg, 1998) classified midlife personalities into three prototypes rated by independent judges. The conflicted prototype, the lowest level, showed personal conflict, psychological problems, poor relationships, anxiety, hostility and rigidity, and was seen as psychologically immature. The traditional prototype showed devotion to others, guilt, emphasis on duties at the expense of self-development, concern with social standards and approval; these women were competent good citizens focused on marriage rather than career but lacked high psychological maturity. The individuated prototype corresponds to Jung's individuation: high autonomy, creativity, closeness to others, self-actualisation, achievement orientation, empathy, tolerance, ego resilience and intellectual and cultural sophistication. Studies in the United States and Australia confirmed that for some women middle age brings personal growth, new directions and freedom to be themselves, supporting Jung's view of individuation as the supreme state of psychological health.

The chapter's Highlights box summarises: introverts are drawn to technical and scientific jobs, extraverts to social ones; introverted, feeling and judging types get higher grades; extraverts score higher on happiness; introverts prefer online contact; and for women, midlife is easier for those with independent careers, and individuation applies to women as well as men.
sections.simple: Dream research found intuitive types recall more archetypal dreams, as Jung predicted. A study of senior executives found behaviour matching individuation. Research on women shows they too go through a midlife reevaluation around 40, that many make major life changes, and that some reach an 'individuated' level of maturity, supporting Jung's ideas.
keyPoints: Cann & Donderi (1986): intuiting types recall more archetypal dreams; introverts more everyday dreams.
Lyons (2002): executives aged 37-55 showed behaviour matching individuation.
Women also experience a midlife crisis; early 40s often the most conflicted period (Helson, 1992).
About two-thirds of college-educated women made major life changes between 37 and 43.
Career-oriented women found midlife easier than those focused on marriage and family (Levinson, 1996).
John, Pals & Westenberg (1998): conflicted, traditional and individuated prototypes.

sections.heading: Reflections on Jung's Theory
sections.detailed:
Contributions. Jung's complex approach has had considerable influence across many disciplines, notably psychiatry, sociology, economics, political science, philosophy and religion. He received honorary degrees from Harvard and Oxford and is acknowledged as a strong influence on many scholars.

Within psychology, his lasting contributions include:
- The word-association test, which became a standard projective technique and inspired the Rorschach inkblot test and lie-detection techniques.
- The concept of psychological complexes, widely accepted today.
- Introversion and extraversion, now widely accepted; scales measuring them are standard diagnostic and selection tools and the subject of much research.
- Individuation, or self-actualisation, which anticipated the work of Abraham Maslow.
- The emphasis on the future in determining behaviour; Jung was the first to stress this, and Alfred Adler adopted the idea.
- Middle age as a time of crucial personality change, an idea embraced by Maslow, Erik Erikson and Raymond Cattell. The midlife crisis is now seen by many as a necessary stage of development and is supported by considerable research.

Criticisms. Despite these contributions, most of Jung's theory was not enthusiastically received by psychologists. One reason is that his concepts are hard to understand. Unlike Freud and Adler, who wrote clearly, Jung did not write for the general public, and his books contain many inconsistencies and contradictions. Jung himself said his thoughts burst out of him like a geyser and that his successors would have to put them in order. One Jungian scholar called a major book of his only partly intelligible, with unclear links between ideas and many internal contradictions; this applies to much of his writing, which lacks internal consistency and systematisation.

The biggest source of criticism is Jung's embrace of the occult and the supernatural. Evidence from mythology and religion is out of favour in an age that treats reason and science as the most legitimate routes to knowledge, and critics charge that Jung accepted his patients' mythical and mystical reports as scientific evidence. Combined with the methodological weaknesses of life-history reconstruction, this means broader parts of the theory, such as the collective unconscious, have resisted scientific validation, even though research supports some ideas on attitudes, functions and types.

Continuing interest. Despite these problems, interest in Jung surged from the late 1980s and continues today. Formal training in Jungian analysis is available in many North American cities and at institutes in South America, Europe and Israel. The Society of Analytical Psychology, founded in 1947, publishes the Journal of Analytical Psychology.
sections.simple: Jung gave psychology lasting ideas: the word-association test, complexes, introversion-extraversion, self-actualisation, the role of the future and the midlife crisis. But his writing is confusing and contradictory, and his reliance on mysticism and the occult makes much of his theory unscientific. Interest in his work has grown again since the late 1980s.
keyPoints: Influence beyond psychology: psychiatry, sociology, economics, political science, philosophy, religion.
Word-association test inspired the Rorschach and lie-detection techniques.
Complexes and introversion-extraversion are widely accepted; individuation anticipated Maslow.
Future orientation adopted by Adler; midlife change embraced by Maslow, Erikson and Cattell.
Criticisms: obscure, inconsistent writing and acceptance of occult and mystical evidence.
Renewed interest since the late 1980s; Jungian training institutes worldwide.

terms.definition: Jung's name for his theory of personality, which broadened libido, stressed future goals and gave the unconscious, including an inherited collective layer, a central role.
For Jung, a broad, generalised psychic or life energy that includes but is not limited to sex; also used more narrowly for the energy that fuels the psyche.
Jung's term for the total personality.
The amount of psychic energy invested in an idea or feeling; high value means the idea strongly influences the person's life.
Every wish or feeling has an opposite; conflict between these polarities generates psychic energy and motivates behaviour, and sharper conflict produces more energy.
Psychic energy is never lost; when invested energy in one area weakens, it shifts to another area of equal value, or into the unconscious if none is found.
A tendency toward balance in the personality, with energy flowing from stronger to weaker values; perfect equal distribution is the ideal but is never reached.
The centre of consciousness, responsible for perceiving, thinking, feeling and remembering; it selectively admits only part of incoming stimuli into awareness.
An attitude in which psychic energy is directed outward, toward the external world and other people; extraverts are open, sociable and assertive.

examples.title: Principle of equivalence: losing interest in cricket
examples.text: A student who spent every evening on cricket gets a knee injury and drifts away from the game. Within months the same intensity shows up in learning guitar. Jung would say the energy did not vanish; it moved to a new area of similar value.

examples.title: Persona: the 'topper' mask
examples.text: A student who is cheerful and confident in class but anxious and unsure at home is wearing a persona. It becomes a problem (inflation of the persona) if they start believing the always-confident version is all they are and stop acknowledging their real worries.

examples.title: A complex in daily life
examples.text: Someone with a status complex may obsess over brands, phone models or job titles, while friends can clearly see the pattern that the person cannot.

examples.title: Shadow: the over-controlled employee
examples.text: A person who never shows anger and suppresses every selfish impulse may come across as flat, then suddenly explode under heavy stress. This mirrors Jung's warning that a fully suppressed shadow can revolt when the ego is weak.

examples.title: Midlife turn inward
examples.text: A 42-year-old engineer with a stable job and family starts feeling that life is empty, then takes up painting and reading philosophy. This is the kind of shift from outer achievement to inner, spiritual interests that Jung described for middle age.
